Vendor of the Week: Tiled — When Design Becomes a Learning Advantage

🏆 Vendor of the Week

Tiled: When Design Becomes a Learning Advantage

How an interactive microapp platform is transforming our curriculum—and why we're running an A/B test to prove that great design actually drives better learning outcomes.

When Anthony Brock from Tiled reached out last month, he didn't send a pitch deck or a capabilities overview—he sent a link to something he'd built using our curriculum. Same introduction, same Unit 1, same frameworks I'd been developing for the Future of PMM program. But the experience of going through it felt completely different from what I'd created: content that animated into view as you scrolled, sections that expanded and collapsed to reveal detail, visual hierarchy that guided your eye through the material in a way that static web pages simply don't. I'd built the original curriculum on a standard web stack—HTML, JavaScript, a Netlify deploy—and it worked fine. People learned from it. But Anthony had taken that same content and wrapped it in something that made the act of learning feel less like reading documentation and more like exploring an app you actually wanted to spend time with.

The result is live: s.tiled.co/2r9iip5/sap-curriculum

The welcome screen. Notice how different this feels from scrolling through documentation.

Tiled, based in Utah, calls these things "microapps"—interactive experiences built from your existing content without writing code. The term is modest. What they've actually built is a container that makes B2B content behave more like consumer media, where the friction between you and the material dissolves and you find yourself three sections deeper than you intended to go. Product marketers spend enormous energy thinking about how to present information to customers—positioning, messaging, the narrative arc of a slide deck—but when it comes to our own internal learning and enablement, we tend to settle for PDFs and wiki pages and formats we'd never accept for customer-facing work. Anthony noticed the gap and built a demo to show me what the curriculum could feel like if we applied the same design thinking we bring to sales content.

Whether It Works

Pretty presentations are easy to dismiss as decoration—visual polish that feels good but doesn't change outcomes. Tiled's customer results suggest something more interesting is happening. IBM reported a 250% increase in content engagement after switching their sales materials to Tiled microapps; Compass Canteen saw a 19% lift in conversion rates. These aren't time-on-page vanity metrics. They're measuring whether people actually do something after consuming the content—click the next step, book the meeting, move to the next stage of a buying process.

"We use Tiled microapps to deepen relationships with our most important accounts. And what would have taken us weeks to create before Tiled, we can now create in a single afternoon."
— Ray Oram, VP of Marketing, IBM

Vendor case studies are curated, of course—the successes get published and the failures disappear—so we're going to run our own experiment with our own content and our own learners, and publish the results either way.

The 72% statistic that frames our "Point of View" section—visual hierarchy that draws the eye to the key insight.

The Test

We're running a straightforward A/B test: same curriculum content, same assessment at the end, different containers. Some learners will go through the standard futureofpmm.com experience; others will go through the Tiled microapp version. We'll track completion rates, time on content, quiz scores, and learner satisfaction through a post-unit survey, and report the results here in about four weeks.

🧪 Our Experiment

Control: Standard futureofpmm.com curriculum (Intro + Unit 1)
Treatment: Tiled microapp version of the same content
Metrics: Completion rate, time on content, quiz scores, learner satisfaction
Reporting: Results published here in 4 weeks

If the Tiled version drives meaningfully better outcomes, we'll have a conversation about rolling it out across the full curriculum. If it doesn't, we'll have learned something important about where design investments actually matter and where content is doing the work regardless of container. The question isn't whether the microapp looks better—it obviously does—but whether that visual sophistication translates into learning outcomes that justify the investment in reformatting everything we've built.
